newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile, United States to start talks on salmon spat.
newsitem.headline: Chile, United States to start talks on salmon spat.

text.p: Fresh salmon, a staple of elegant buffets, barbecues and brunches, will top the agenda at trade talks this week between Chilean and U.S. officials as they grapple with an increasingly bitter dispute over fish.

Producers in Maine and Oregon accuse Chile of dumping salmon on the U.S. market, where the fish has gone from a luxury item to a supermarket standard in the space of a few years thanks largely to Chile's booming output.

Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia flew to Washington this weekend for talks Tuesday with U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley on the dumping charges, which threaten to cripple one of Chile's star exports.

The charges, which received their first hearing July 3 in the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), have provoked an angry response in Chile, where businessmen accuse the United States of punishing them for efficiency and market savvy.

"As long as we were at one or two percent of the market, they didn't mind. Now that we're big players in the market, we get what you might call political opposition," said Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza.

Chilean officials compare the row to the 1989 grapes scare, when protesters pelted the U.S. embassy with grapes after American food inspectors found two Chilean grapes injected with cyanide and banned the country's fruit for five days. Chilean growers, still fuming over the episode, saw it as a trick to discredit their product.
"It's no coincidence that after first facing the case of the grapes, we now see the same thing with salmon," said Garcia.
Chile will expect the Clinton administration to fight the U.S. salmon producers' charges if it wants to prove it's sincere about its wish to extend free trade to all the Americas, said Garcia.

The ITC is scheduled to rule on July 24 whether the dumping charges merit investigation. If it does, the ruling could lead to compensatory tariffs and surcharges on Chilean salmon imports into the United States, which last year totalled 41,000 tonnes or just over half of U.S. consumption of farmed salmon.

The head of Chile's top business group Sofofa, Felipe Lamarca, denounced the dumping charges in a blistering, nationalistic tirade which gave a hint of the tone Washington can expect if the conflict worsens.

"I have the duty to defend Chile and defend Chilean industry against the economic aggression coming from the United States," said Lamarca. "They're showing disrespect for our economic and social sovereignty."
Salmon and trout exports to the United States soared from about $3.4 million in 1986 to $177 million last year.
Total Chilean salmon production has climbed from zero in the 1970s -- the fish is not native to South America -- to become the world's second largest producer after Norway.

What makes their salmon so cheap, say local producers, is that Chile is also the world's second largest producer after Peru of fishmeal, the salmons' ground-up cousins and their staple food. North American and European raisers must import fishmeal, greatly raising their costs.
Fattened up on fishmeal, salmon does well in cages in the fjords and bays of southern Chile, where the industry has become a major employer.
But U.S. producers allege Chilean salmon is cheaper because of tax breaks and government handouts which they say allow producers to sell at artifically low prices.

Of the 30 incentive programs for Chilean salmon cited by the U.S. producers as thinly-veiled subsidies, the ITC agreed at the July 3 meeting to investigate 21 as possible breaches of fair trade practices. They include credit lines for capital goods, loan guarantees and promotional spending, all from the Chilean government.

Chile says all the programs are in line with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Garcia, quoted in the Santiago newspaper Estrategia, admitted two of the programs were subsidies, but would be phased out before a WTO deadline in the year 2002.
Chilean raisers say they don't compete directly with Maine and Oregon because Chile sells de-boned salmon, an essentially different product from the American version with bones intact.
The Chilean product appeals more to backyard cooks and sandwich makers, while American salmon is the favorite of restaurants where chefs prefer to do the cutting and de-boning themselves.

If that argument doesn't work, the Chileans have also told the United States they will appeal to the WTO and may seek support from the Mercosur trade bloc led by Brazil and Argentina, of which Chile is an associate member.
